rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the Quran’s only account of Moses without a corresponding reference in Biblical text.
rows.anchor: This is the only account of Moses in the Quran that does not also have some reference in the Biblical text

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unnamed servant is identified by commentators and a Prophetic hadith as Khiḍr, widely regarded as a prophet associated with life beyond ordinary limits.
rows.anchor: The mysterious servant is not named in the Quran, but is identified by all commentators and by a ḥadīth of the Prophet as Khiḍr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s longevity and “greening” associate him with perpetual life and realms between life and death.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr is considered widely to be a prophet who lives well beyond the ordinary span of a human lifetime

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufis regard Khiḍr as an initiator into divine mysteries and a spiritual guide; Ibn ʿArabī said he received initiation from him.
rows.anchor: In Sufism, Khiḍr is considered the prophet of initiation into Divine mysteries as well as a special spiritual guide

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story shares the sūrah’s intermediate-realm theme: life and death, exoteric and esoteric knowledge, the two seas, and Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s barriers.
rows.anchor: this story shares the theme of intermediate realms: between life and death, between exoteric and esoteric knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading presents a dramatic demonstration of God’s power over life, death, and resurrection, as in the youths’ story.
rows.anchor: It provides one of the most dramatic demonstrations of God’s power over life, death, and resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story can symbolize the difference between exoteric knowledge from scripture or reason and esoteric knowledge received directly from God.
rows.anchor: a symbolic account of the difference between formal and exoteric knowledge based upon revealed scripture or reason

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story also symbolizes spiritual mastery, discipleship, and levels of the human soul and its training.
rows.anchor: a symbolic account of spiritual mastery and discipleship and of the different levels of the human soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account shows God’s Will operating mysteriously through events, whose hidden taʾwīl is known only to a few such as Khiḍr.
rows.anchor: God’s Will is mysteriously operating through all events and actions and attests to the existence of a hidden interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses represents religion’s outward or exoteric dimension.
rows.anchor: Moses, who in this story represents the exoteric, or outward, dimension of religion

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Commentators widely identify Moses’ servant as Joshua.
rows.anchor: Moses’ servant is widely identified as Joshua (Q, R, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatā can mean a youth or young man, not only a servant.
rows.anchor: Servant translates fatā, which can also mean simply a youth or a young man

rows.speaker: Q, R, Z
rows.claim: A Prophetic hadith recommends addressing slaves or servants as “my young man/woman” rather than “my slave/servant.”
rows.anchor: the Prophet instructed people to refer to their slaves or servants as my “young man”

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Here fatā reflects younger Joshua’s service to Moses and learning from him.
rows.anchor: in this case, the term refers to the fact that the younger Joshua followed Moses, served him, and gained knowledge from him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is Joshua’s master and sets the journey’s goals; later Moses becomes Khiḍr’s disciple, while Khiḍr serves only God.
rows.anchor: Moses is the master and Joshua the disciple, and it is Moses who sets the goals and parameters for their journey

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two seas literally signify river fresh water meeting salt sea water.
rows.anchor: In the Quran, the two seas are understood in the most literal sense to refer to the freshwater of rivers and the saltwater of the seas

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran describes a barrier between the waters where they mingle without one transgressing into the other.
rows.anchor: the point where the two meet as the site of an impenetrable “barrier”

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Suggested junction locations include the Persian and Roman seas or Tangiers; the proposals can be geographically impossible or vague.
rows.anchor: such as the meeting point of the Persian sea (perhaps the Persian Gulf) and the Roman sea

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The geographic site is immaterial; Moses seeks it because he was told he would meet someone more knowledgeable there.
rows.anchor: The geographical location, however, is ultimately immaterial to the story. Rather, Moses seeks this junction, because he was told

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Z
rows.claim: A report says Moses claimed to be the most knowledgeable when asked, so God directed him through Gabriel to a more knowledgeable servant at the junction.
rows.anchor: Moses was once questioned by his people as to who was most knowledgeable, and he replied that he was

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Some commentators interpret the two seas as Moses and Khiḍr, each representing a sea of knowledge.
rows.anchor: Some commentators suggest that the two seas here refer to Moses and Khiḍr themselves as representatives of two “seas of knowledge”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the allegory, freshwater’s linearity represents rational thought and revealed law guiding toward salvation or God.
rows.anchor: The freshwater rivers, with their linear and directional nature, symbolize rational thought and knowledge of the Divine Law

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The salt sea’s depth and unpredictability represent inner knowledge and infinite divine knowledge that linear human reasoning cannot penetrate.
rows.anchor: the saltwater sea, with its vastness, unpredictable currents, and fathomless depth, symbolizes deep inner knowledge

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: As a soul allegory, the two seas can represent the worlds of spirit and body, with the soul as their meeting point.
rows.anchor: the two seas can refer to the world of the spirit and the world of bodies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Joshua did not recognize the junction when they reached it; there they forgot the fish, which escaped to sea.
rows.anchor: the story suggests that they did not recognize this junction when they reached it and that it is at this point that they forgot their fish

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: The fish’s revival at the junction signals Khiḍr’s presence, whose greening signifies transcendent life and agelessness.
rows.anchor: The fact that the fish was revived in that place is an indication of Khiḍr’s presence there

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Z
rows.claim: A report places Moses and Joshua sleeping by a rock at a spring of life, unaware it was their destination.
rows.anchor: Moses and Joshua settled down to sleep by a rock near a spring referred to as the “spring of life”

rows.speaker: Q, Th, Z
rows.claim: The carried fish was salted and preserved, and they had already eaten some of it.
rows.anchor: The fish they were carrying in a basket was said to have been a salted and preserved fish, and Moses and Joshua had already eaten from it

rows.speaker: Q, R, Z
rows.claim: One account says water splashed onto the fish accidentally as Moses or Joshua performed ablutions, reviving it.
rows.anchor: when Moses or Joshua accidentally splashed the fish with some water as they were making their ablutions for prayer

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another account says spring water reached the basket, reanimated the fish, overturned the basket, and let it escape.
rows.anchor: water from the stream, coming from the “spring of life,” flowed near the basket, reaching and reanimating the fish inside

rows.speaker: JJ, Q
rows.claim: Commentators say the fish burrowed a tunnel to the sea while the sea water was miraculously held back from it.
rows.anchor: the water from the sea was miraculously held back from the tunnel, allowing the fish to travel through it to the sea

rows.speaker: K, Z
rows.claim: After passing the junction and spring of life, Moses felt hunger and weariness and asked Joshua for their fish meal.
rows.anchor: Having left the junction and the spring of life, Moses began to experience hunger and weariness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The missed junction can signify a barzakh, a liminal realm without space or extension.
rows.anchor: this junction represents a barzakh, a liminal place between two worlds or realms, which itself has no space or extension

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some say God induced Moses’ hunger to remind him of the fish and make him return.
rows.anchor: Some suggest that God induced Moses’ hunger in order to remind him of the fish

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: In a soul allegory, the junction resembles the womb, where Moses is nourished without need; passing beyond symbolizes birth into worldly need and hardship.
rows.anchor: Moses was sustained like a child in the mother’s womb, having no need to eat or struggle

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Joshua’s “Didst thou see?” introduces his marvelous account rather than asking a real question, since Moses had not seen the fish escape.
rows.anchor: Didst thou see? is not meant as a question, for Joshua knew that Moses had not witnessed the loss of the fish

rows.speaker: JJ, R
rows.claim: Some reports say Joshua knew the lost fish was the sign of arrival, but fell asleep after seeing it escape and forgot.
rows.anchor: according to some reports, he even knew that losing their fish was to be a sign that they had reached their destination

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Joshua excused his failure to tell Moses by saying Satan caused him to neglect the matter.
rows.anchor: Joshua attempted to excuse his oversight by claiming it was Satan who had caused him to neglect to mention the matter

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Moses immediately recognized, or in some accounts had already been told, that the fish’s escape site was their destination and Khiḍr’s meeting place.
rows.anchor: as he immediately realized—or according to some accounts was apprised beforehand (R, Ṭ)—that the place where the fish was lost

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: In the soul allegory, Moses’ retracing his steps symbolizes return to God and restoration of primordial fiṭrah.
rows.anchor: Moses retracing his steps represents the spiritual journey back to God, reversing the “fall” into worldly existence

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: Commentators identify the servant as Khiḍr on the basis of hadith reports.
rows.anchor: The servant from among Our servants is identified by all commentators as Khiḍr on the basis of aḥādīth

rows.speaker: Q, R, Th
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s name, “the Green One,” is explained by greenery appearing wherever he prayed or stood; Persian miniatures portray him in green.
rows.anchor: wherever he prayed or stood, everything around him became green

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Khiḍr is widely considered a prophet.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr is widely considered a prophet (Q, R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some commentators instead say Khiḍr was a righteous servant or an angel.
rows.anchor: some say that he was just a righteous servant of God or an angel (Q)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: His direct, unmediated knowledge from God is offered as evidence that Khiḍr was a prophet.
rows.anchor: he was given direct and unmediated knowledge from God, which is the mark of prophethood

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Another argument for Khiḍr’s prophethood is that Moses sought knowledge from and followed him; only a prophet can outrank a prophet.
rows.anchor: none can be superior to a prophet save another prophet

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s statement that he did not act on his own command is treated as a prophetic mark, linked to 21:27.
rows.anchor: another mark of prophethood, as in 21:27: They precede Him not in speech

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The hidden realities behind Khiḍr’s shocking acts are said to be knowable only through revelation received by prophets.
rows.anchor: the inner meaning of acts and events known by Khiḍr (see vv. 78–82) can only be known through Divine revelation

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: One report places Khiḍr on a green carpet over water, where Moses greeted him with peace.
rows.anchor: Moses found Khiḍr seated or lying on a green carpet upon the water and enshrouded in his robe

rows.speaker: Q, Th
rows.claim: In some accounts Khiḍr uncovered his face and asked whether there was peace in Moses’ land and who Moses was.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr removed the part of the robe covering his face and asked, “Is there peace in your land? Who are you?”

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another account says Khiḍr recognized Moses immediately and greeted him as Israel’s prophet.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr immediately recognized Moses and greeted him as the “prophet of the Children of Israel”

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Some accounts place Khiḍr’s life in the eras of Afarīdūn, Dhu’l-Qarnayn, and Moses.
rows.anchor: Some consider Khiḍr to have been alive at the time of the legendary Persian hero and king Afarīdūn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr remains a Sufi figure whom some believe guides or initiates people through dreams and visions.
rows.anchor: some of whom consider him to be an eternal and mysterious mystical master who still guides or even initiates certain people

rows.speaker: Q, R, Z
rows.claim: Many interpret the mercy granted to Khiḍr as prophethood.
rows.anchor: many understand as a reference to prophethood

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the mercy a spiritual perfection that frees Khiḍr from base matter and grants perpetual life.
rows.anchor: a kind of spiritual perfection that allows him to remain completely unencumbered by base matter

rows.speaker: JJ, Q, Z
rows.claim: Knowledge from God’s Presence is widely understood as knowledge of the Unseen, which belongs only to God.
rows.anchor: which is widely understood to mean knowledge of the Unseen, which lies only with God

rows.speaker: K, Q, R, Su, Qu
rows.claim: The knowledge is inner and universal truth disclosed directly, without human teacher or effort, through divine inspiration.
rows.anchor: without the intermediary of a human teacher (K, R, Su)—acquired through Divine inspiration rather than through human effort

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Al-Ghazzālī and other Sufis use ʿilm ladunī for knowledge of unveiling, ʿilm al-mukāshafah.
rows.anchor: “knowledge from God’s Presence”(ʿilm ladunī; R)

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Junayd calls Khiḍr’s knowledge an unveiling of lights from the recesses of the Unseen.
rows.anchor: as the “unveiling of lights from the recesses of the Unseen”(Su)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s paired gift of mercy and knowledge echoes the youths’ prayer for mercy from God’s Presence.
rows.anchor: echoes the supplication of the youths of the cave in v. 10, where they pray to God seeking mercy from Thy Presence

rows.speaker: IK, R, Z
rows.claim: Khiḍr says God gave Moses knowledge withheld from him, while Moses had knowledge Khiḍr lacked; they are two seas of knowledge.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr told Moses that God had given him knowledge that He had not given to Moses

rows.speaker: al-Sulamī
rows.claim: Al-Sulamī says Moses surpassed Khiḍr in what he received from God, while Khiḍr surpassed Moses in other knowledge.
rows.anchor: although Moses was more knowledgeable than Khiḍr in what Moses had taken from God, Khiḍr was more knowledgeable in other ways

rows.speaker: al-Sulamī
rows.claim: Al-Sulamī contrasts Moses’ subsistence in truth with Khiḍr’s annihilation in it, Sufi stations called baqāʾ and fanāʾ.
rows.anchor: although Moses “subsisted” in the truth, Khiḍr was annihilated in it

rows.speaker: IK, Th
rows.claim: Khiḍr compares both men’s knowledge to a sparrow’s tiny sip beside God’s knowledge.
rows.anchor: My knowledge or your knowledge, compared with the Knowledge of God, is naught but the small amount of water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ request to follow Khiḍr displays humility, sincere desire for inner knowledge, and willingness to learn despite his prophetic status.
rows.anchor: Moses’ genuine quest for inner knowledge for its own sake, his lack of pride, and his willingness to humble himself

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says even prophets lack all knowledge: above every knower is another knower; Moses models humility, linked to 12:76.
rows.anchor: even great prophets, such as Moses, do not possess all knowledge, for above every possessor of knowledge is a knower

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ humility rebukes the idolatrous Makkans, whose arrogance contrasts with his sincere learning from Khiḍr.
rows.anchor: serve as a moral rebuke to the idolatrous Makkans, whose arrogance and rejection of the revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks for sound judgment; the cave youths likewise ask God for sound judgment in their affairs.
rows.anchor: in v. 10, the youths of the cave also pray to God to grant them sound judgment in their affairs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s prediction is truthful, not merely protest, and foreshadows their parting.
rows.anchor: is not merely a protest, but a statement of truth and a foreshadowing of Moses and Khiḍr’s parting

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs
rows.claim: Moses cannot endure Khiḍr because Moses serves revealed law while Khiḍr performs acts that seem contrary to law but have inner significance.
rows.anchor: Moses has been sent as a prophet of the Divine Law, while Khiḍr has been entrusted with some acts that seem outwardly to be contrary to that Law

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their different vocations allow only brief companionship, like waters meeting temporarily at a barzakh, lest either compromise the other’s mission.
rows.anchor: Like the water of the two seas that briefly comingle at the junction, or barzakh, between them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What humans encompass of divine knowledge depends on God’s will, as 2:255 says.
rows.anchor: what one encompasses of Divine Knowledge is a matter of God’s Will and choosing

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Moses knows outward justice and righteousness but not the Unseen knowledge granted to Khiḍr.
rows.anchor: Moses has only been taught what is just and righteous with regard to the outward and apparent reality of things

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Some Sufis say Moses’ bodily and temporal limits veil unseen truths, while ageless Khiḍr seems free of bodily decay.
rows.anchor: Moses, unlike Khiḍr, is bound by time and the limits of the material body

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Moses’ promise of patience expresses strong preparedness and sincere seeking.
rows.anchor: because of the strength of Moses’ preparedness to receive this knowledge and the sincerity of his seeking

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Moses’ “if God wills” acknowledges that future events depend on God’s will.
rows.anchor: acknowledging that all future events depend on God’s Will

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is likewise advised not to promise future action without acknowledging God’s will.
rows.anchor: where the Prophet Muhammad is advised never to promise anything in the future without acknowledging God’s Will

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī reads Khiḍr’s no-questions condition as proper student etiquette toward a teacher or master.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr’s request indicates the proper etiquette that a student should demonstrate toward a teacher

rows.speaker: K, R
rows.claim: A disciple who trusts the guide should follow and wait for the teacher to decide when spiritual truths may be sought.
rows.anchor: it is for Moses only to follow his teacher’s path; it is not for him to seek out spiritual truths

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The teacher or master must account for the student’s needs and capacity when choosing a lesson.
rows.anchor: the master assumes the responsibility for taking into account the needs and capabilities of the student

rows.speaker: IK, Th, Z
rows.claim: The ship’s owner reportedly recognized Khiḍr as a prophet and gave them passage without charge.
rows.anchor: whose owner reportedly recognized Khiḍr as a prophet and therefore allowed them to ride without charge

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: In a soul allegory, the ship is the body carrying the soul through material life and enabling worship; damaging it symbolizes ascetic discipline.
rows.anchor: the ship may then symbolize the body, which carries individuals across the sea of material existence

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s reminder means the resolve required to follow this path must be stronger.
rows.anchor: which is a warning that one’s resolve must be stronger if one is to follow such a path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ plea about forgetting recalls the believers’ prayer in 2:286 not to be taken to task for forgetting or error.
rows.anchor: recalls 2:286, where the believers pray, Our Lord, take us not to task if we forget or err

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Khiḍr reportedly killed the boy by striking him in the head with a stone.
rows.anchor: reportedly by striking him in the head with a stone

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Moses views the boy as innocent, sinless, and unlawfully killed, contrary to Mosaic law; he considers this worse than damaging the ship.
rows.anchor: a young, innocent boy who had slain no other soul or even committed a major sin

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Mystically, the slain boy symbolizes the evil-inclined soul overcome by conquering anger and other passions.
rows.anchor: the slain boy represents the soul that inclines toward evil and is “slain” when one overcomes the anger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr repeats his warning, Moses repents, and this exchange anticipates their final parting.
rows.anchor: also anticipates the ultimate parting of ways between Moses and Khiḍr in v. 78

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses admits he has already given Khiḍr sufficient reason to leave because he twice broke the no-question condition.
rows.anchor: he has already given Khiḍr sufficient justification to leave his company

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some identify the town as Antioch or Eilat.
rows.anchor: which some speculate may have been Antioch or Eilat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The townspeople refuse hospitality; Khiḍr repairs a leaning wall as they leave.
rows.anchor: refused to show them any hospitality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ remark about wages implicitly questions why Khiḍr repaired the wall for an inhospitable town without payment.
rows.anchor: contains an implicit question about why Khiḍr sought no compensation for the good deed

rows.speaker: Su, K
rows.claim: Commentators teach that seeking worldly reward for a good deed cancels its spiritual merit; virtue should be sought for its own sake.
rows.anchor: doing a good deed and then seeking worldly reward for it nullifies the spiritual merit of the good deed

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Some say Moses’ last protest arose from his hunger and desire, unlike earlier objections made for others’ welfare.
rows.anchor: his protest in this case arose from his own hunger and desire

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: In the soul allegory, the repaired wall symbolizes the restored tranquil soul, perfected in virtue after passions are subdued.
rows.anchor: passions and the lower soul have been subdued (K)

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: The parting is inevitable: Moses did not refrain from questioning, and Khiḍr no longer had patience to remain with him.
rows.anchor: when Moses did not prove to be patient enough to refrain from questioning Khiḍr’s actions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their meeting, like the two seas’ junction, is temporary; law and timeless truth retain distinct vocations despite brief mingling.
rows.anchor: The junction between these “two seas of knowledge” (see 18:60c), like the junction between the two physical seas, can only be a temporary meeting

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī says Moses wanted to continue learning, while Khiḍr preferred solitude with God over company of creatures.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr preferred to leave Moses’ company, preferring solitude with God to the company of created beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr offers the taʾwīl, or hidden wisdom, of his acts; later tradition uses taʾwīl for scripture’s inner meaning, as in 3:7.
rows.anchor: Taʾwīl is translated both here and in 3:7 simply as “interpretation,” but in later Islamic tradition this term is often used

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If taʾwīl is esoteric meaning, events and scripture have hidden meanings known to God and those granted knowledge from His Presence.
rows.anchor: there is a hidden or esoteric meaning to all phenomena and events as well as to what God has revealed in sacred scriptures

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s ability to explain his acts indicates Moses’ soul was purified and strengthened to receive their spiritual meaning and encounter the Unseen.
rows.anchor: Moses’ soul had been purified and strengthened enough for the reception of the spiritual meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr’s damage preserved the ship from a tyrant king who seized sound vessels; the lesser harm was preferable to permanent confiscation.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr explained that his act of damaging the ship was actually a means of saving it

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A moral lesson is to choose the lesser harm when forced between two harms.
rows.anchor: when forced to choose between two harmful things, one should choose the least harmful

rows.speaker: al-Kāshānī
rows.claim: The damaged ship symbolizes disciplining the body to prevent its seizure by the lower soul inclined to evil.
rows.anchor: symbolizes the “breaking” of the body through spiritual exercise and asceticism in order to prevent the body from being “seized”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ship’s apparent destruction parallels infant Moses’ basket journey: an apparent danger becomes deliverance from Pharaoh’s order to seize and kill Israelite boys.
rows.anchor: the casting of the infant Moses into the water in a basket—an act that may have seemed likely to result in his death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy’s killing spares believing parents the future distress of his rebellion and disbelief, though they could only experience his death as tragedy.
rows.anchor: his parents would not yet have witnessed rebellion and disbelief from him and thus could only have considered his death a tragedy

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr cites a hadith that God decrees nothing for a believer except what is better for that believer.
rows.anchor: God does not decree anything for a believer, save that it is better for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses objects under law protecting innocents; Khiḍr’s explanation presents the killing as divinely commanded wisdom and mercy.
rows.anchor: Moses’ objection to Khiḍr’s slaying of the boy is based upon the religious law that forbids the killing of innocents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story distinguishes prescriptive Sacred Law from God’s ultimate decree beyond human understanding, inviting reflection on divine will and human justice.
rows.anchor: the difference between God’s Will for human beings as discerned through the prescriptive commands found in Sacred Law and revelation

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: The buried treasure might be wealth or knowledge; knowledge is plausible because, like taʾwīl, it was hidden from Moses’ outward sight.
rows.anchor: hidden or “buried” for the boys to discover later, when they were capable of understanding it

rows.speaker: al-Kāshānī
rows.claim: The restored wall symbolizes the tranquil soul; its buried treasure is spiritual knowledge in the heart, accessible when soul and intellect mature beyond bodily temptation.
rows.anchor: Reading the story as an analogy for the soul, al-Kāshānīsuggests that the repaired wall symbolizes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khiḍr says he acted on God’s command, whose will remains inscrutable without the hidden interpretation of events.
rows.anchor: he did not act upon his own command, indicating that he was acting upon the Command or Will of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Linking this taʾwīl with 3:7 suggests scripture and worldly events contain meanings known to God and perhaps a few servants.
rows.anchor: whatever one encounters, either in scripture or in the world, contains a meaning that is known only to God

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says prophets judge outward appearances, citing the Prophet’s hadith that judgment is outward while God knows inward secrets; Khiḍr judged true purposes.
rows.anchor: We judge according to the outward; and God is responsible for the inward

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says God sent Moses to Khiḍr after Moses mastered outward sharīʿah, to learn the inward realities; religious learning moves from outward law to inward truth.
rows.anchor: the proper trajectory for religious knowledge is for people to move from a mastery of the science of sharīʿah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Makkans asked about Dhu’l-Qarnayn on Jewish scholars’ advice while testing Muhammad’s prophethood; one report says People of the Book asked directly.
rows.anchor: the Makkans questioned the Prophet on the advice of some Jewish scholars

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One report says some People of the Book directly questioned the Prophet about Dhu’l-Qarnayn.
rows.anchor: some of the People of the Book came to the Prophet directly to ask him about Dhu’l-Qarnayn

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs, R
rows.claim: A hadith calls Dhu’l-Qarnayn a youth from Rūm who built Alexandria, identifying him as Alexander son of Philip.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth identifies Dhu’l-Qarnayn as a youth from Rūm (i.e., from the western lands) who built the Egyptian city of Alexandria

rows.speaker: Ṭb
rows.claim: Some modern Islamic scholars identify Dhu’l-Qarnayn with Cyrus the Great rather than Alexander.
rows.anchor: some Islamic scholars of the modern period have identified him with the ancient Persian king Cyrus the Great

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: A hadith says an angel took Dhu’l-Qarnayn into the sky to view the whole earth and its surrounding fathomless sea.
rows.anchor: Dhu’l-Qarnayn was visited by an angel who ascended with him through the sky until he could see the whole of the earth

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Some say Dhu’l-Qarnayn was a righteous servant granted worldly sovereignty, knowledge, and wisdom.
rows.anchor: simply a righteous servant of God to whom God granted sovereignty over the world along with knowledge and wisdom

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Others consider him a prophet.
rows.anchor: Others suggest that he was a prophet

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Still others say he was an angel.
rows.anchor: or an angel

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: He is described as one who loved God and was loved by God.
rows.anchor: He is described as one who loved God and whom God loved

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Clouds, light, and darkness served him: light guided him by night and darkness shielded his rear.
rows.anchor: The clouds, and even light and darkness themselves, were said to have been placed at his service

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: One theory says “two horns” were physical horns; after preaching one God, he was killed and resurrected after blows to each horn, with accounts differing on a second resurrection.
rows.anchor: Some suggest that he had on his head what appeared to be two horns

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he ruled both Rūm and Persia.
rows.anchor: Other accounts say this name refers to his being the king of both Rūm and Persia

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: A hadith interpretation derives the title from journeys around the earth’s eastern and western “horns.”
rows.anchor: according to a ḥadīth, it refers to his journeys, which are said to have circled around both “horns” of the earth

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some reports say he dreamed of approaching the sun and grasping its eastern and western horns, after which people named him Dhu’l-Qarnayn.
rows.anchor: Some report that he had a dream in which he drew near to the sun

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Other accounts say both sides of his head were copper.
rows.anchor: Still others mention that the two sides of his head were made of copper

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Another account says he wore a horned headdress or helmet.
rows.anchor: or that he wore a headdress or helmet with two horns at the side

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Some understand the title simply as praise for his courage and fearlessness.
rows.anchor: it was simply a title he was given as a way of indicating his bravery and fearlessness

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some derive the title from living two centuries, though that conflicts with Alexander’s short life.
rows.anchor: Some suggest that his name means that he lived for two centuries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two-century etymology conflicts with the historical Alexander, who died young.
rows.anchor: this is inconsistent with the historical Alexander, who died quite young

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: God’s establishment of Dhu’l-Qarnayn in the land is understood as making the terrain smooth and easy for travel and conquest.
rows.anchor: That God established Dhu’l-Qarnayn in the land means that He made the land smooth and easy for him

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some understand the means granted to Dhu’l-Qarnayn as knowledge of all things.
rows.anchor: which most understand to mean a knowledge of all things

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Others understand the means as power and tools to acquire whatever he wanted.
rows.anchor: as well as the power and the tools with which to acquire all that he desired
